opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key insight is really about where the training signal comes from. With classic RLHF, you train a reward model on human preference data, and then you optimize the LLM against that reward model. The problem is that the reward model is itself a learned approximation, so it can be gamed. The model figures out what the reward model likes, maybe longer answers, a certain tone, confident phrasing, and that doesn't necessarily mean the answer is more correct. That's reward hacking, and it limits how long you can run the optimization before things degrade.

With verifiable rewards, you swap the learned reward model for something deterministic. For a math problem you check whether the final answer matches the known solution. For code you run it against test cases or see if it compiles. It's essentially binary, right or wrong, and much harder to fool. That lets you scale up reinforcement learning a lot further, because the signal stays honest even as the model gets better.

What I find most interesting, and what we saw with DeepSeek-R1 and the R1-Zero experiments, is that you only reward the final answer, not the reasoning steps. You don't tell the model how to think. Yet when you optimize for correctness, the model learns on its own to produce longer chains of thought, to double-check its work, to backtrack when something looks off. Those reasoning behaviors emerge because they help it get the right answer more often. To me that's remarkable: you get reasoning almost as a side effect of a very simple, cheap, reliable signal.

It's also practical. You don't need armies of annotators labeling preferences or writing step-by-step explanations. If you have problems with checkable answers, you can generate a lot of training signal cheaply.

The caveat is that it works best in domains where verification is easy: math, code, logic puzzles. For open-ended things like creative writing or nuanced advice, there's no simple correctness check, so you still need preference-based methods or some hybrid. But for reasoning specifically, verifiable rewards were a big unlock, and I think that's why they've become so central in how these models are trained now.

r001.rationale: The response says math answers can be checked against a known solution, but does not explain that mathematically equivalent written forms can both be accepted.

r002.rationale: It says deterministic verification makes the signal cheap and scalable, and that checkable problems can generate “a lot of training signal cheaply,” conveying scalable reward scoring.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a learned reward model that can be gamed and may reward traits unrelated to correctness with deterministic verification that is harder to fool.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing with verifiable rewards is that they let you get around the biggest bottleneck in post-training, which is the reward signal itself. If you look at how we did RLHF for the last few years, you had to collect human preference data, train a reward model on it, and then optimize against that reward model. And that works, but it has two problems. One, it's expensive and slow, because you need humans in the loop. And two, the reward model is a learned approximation, so it can be gamed. The policy finds weird outputs that the reward model likes but that aren't actually good, and you get reward hacking.

With verifiable rewards, you sidestep both of those. If you're training on math problems, you can just check whether the final answer matches. If it's code, you run the unit tests. There's no learned judge to fool, and you don't need people labeling anything. So you can generate as many samples as you want, score them automatically, and scale the RL stage in a way that was really hard before.

And I think what DeepSeek-R1 showed, and that's why it got so much attention, is that with just this kind of simple, rule-based reward, the model learns to produce these long chains of thought on its own. Nobody told it to write out intermediate steps or to go back and check its work. That behavior emerged because the training signal rewarded correct final answers, and the model figured out that reasoning more carefully is the way to get there. That's a very different picture from supervised fine-tuning, where you're basically showing the model examples of reasoning and hoping it imitates them.

Now, the honest caveat is that this works best in domains where you actually have a verifier. Math and code are the obvious ones. For something like writing or open-ended advice, it's much harder to say what "correct" means, so you're back to learned reward models or some hybrid. But even there, I think the reasoning skills picked up in the verifiable domains seem to transfer to some degree, which is one of the more interesting open questions right now. So I see verifiable rewards less as the whole story and more as the foundation that made reasoning models practical to train at scale.

r001.rationale: It says math answers can be checked against the final answer, but does not explain that equivalent answers in different written forms can count as correct.

r002.rationale: It says answers can be scored automatically and that this lets training generate and score as many samples as desired.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a learned reward model that can be gamed with direct checks of math answers or code tests, presenting verification as a more reliable correctness signal.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that, for some tasks, checking an answer is much easier than generating it. If a model writes code, we can run that code against tests. If it solves a math problem, we can often check whether the final answer is correct. That gives us a concrete training signal without needing a person to evaluate every response.

With reinforcement learning, the model can generate different solutions and get rewarded for the ones that work. We don’t necessarily have to tell it exactly what each intermediate step should look like. That leaves room for it to learn useful behaviors, like checking its work or trying a different approach when it gets stuck.

The caveat is that the verifier defines what you’re rewarding. Passing a few tests doesn’t mean the code is correct in every situation, and getting the right final answer doesn’t guarantee that every reasoning step was sound. But when verification is reliable, it gives us a scalable way to train toward correctness, rather than just toward answers that sound convincing.

r001.rationale: It says math answers can often be checked for correctness, but does not explain that symbolic verification accepts mathematically equivalent answers with different written forms.

r002.rationale: It describes a scalable training signal and rewarding solutions that work, but does not clearly state that cheap, deterministic verification can score very large numbers of generated answers.

r003.rationale: It contrasts verification with answers that merely sound convincing, but does not compare deterministic answer verification with an approximate reward-model score.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that, with reasoning, there can be many different ways to arrive at a correct answer. You don’t necessarily want to prescribe every intermediate step. You want to give the model room to explore different approaches, but you still need a reliable signal about whether an approach worked.

With something like a math problem, you can check the final answer. With code, you can run tests. That gives you a reward signal that’s much less subjective than asking another model whether a response looks good. A response can sound very convincing and still be wrong.

And that’s useful for reinforcement learning because you can sample different solutions and reinforce the ones that actually succeed. The caveat is that your verifier has to measure what you care about. Passing a few tests doesn’t mean a program is correct in every case, and getting the right answer doesn’t guarantee that every reasoning step is valid. But where verification works well, it gives you a very practical way to improve reasoning without having to manually write out all the reasoning examples.

r001.rationale: It says math answers can be checked, but does not explain that symbolically equivalent answers count as correct despite different written forms.

r002.rationale: It describes sampling different solutions, but does not say that verification is cheap or deterministic enough to score very large numbers of generated answers.

r003.rationale: It contrasts checking answers with tests against asking another model whether a response looks good, describing verification as a less subjective and more reliable correctness signal.
